name: Jamal Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays anonymous. Can you walk me through an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a claims handler, the junior kind, at Keystone, an insurer that only covers landlords. Burst pipes, tenants who leave a flat wrecked, a boiler that floods the downstairs neighbour. I log the claim, check the landlord's policy, get the plumber's or builder's quote in and sort out whether it's covered.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the practical side, seeing how buildings actually go wrong. I use AI every day, for drafting letters and reading builders' quotes, and I'm usually first to try anything new the company brings in. The hard part is I'm not careful enough yet. I approved a full kitchen refit last month when the policy only covered the units that were damaged, and Mrs Okafor, my manager, had to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use it as a tool already, so if it stays a tool, nothing much changes for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: work hard, use what helps, and stop waiting for someone else to fix things. Online I'd post the odd thing about how I use it for builders' quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in decent shape. Nadia, my wife, has her home baking business going, we've got about four months saved, and Keystone's busy because there are more landlords every year. My only real worry is getting sloppy on the policy limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Keystone and get my head round the policy wording so I stop making refit mistakes. I'd keep helping my cousin Yusuf with his property maintenance jobs on Saturdays, because it's good money and I learn the trade. We'd keep putting a bit aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that bothers you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen refit thing, honestly. I don't want to be known as the fast guy who costs Keystone money. That's my pride, more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with your cousin's maintenance work in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd grow, I think. Yusuf's got more work than he can handle, and I know claims from the inside, so I can tell landlords what their insurer will and won't pay for.

think: I'm in **decent shape**: my wife's baking business, four months saved, a busy employer.

steps.text: Study Keystone's policy limits so refit errors stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I believe. Keystone's already testing a system that reads the quotes and decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind. I'd say it kindly to the older ones, but I'd say it. And I'd say the people who build things will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the claims team shrinks, no question. Logging, checking, writing letters, all on your list. I'm good with the tools but I'm junior and I make mistakes, so I could easily be one of the ones who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to be on the test team for the new system, because I'd learn how insurers will decide claims from now on. Then I'd go bigger with Yusuf: a small maintenance firm that does insurance repairs for landlords, with me handling the claims side using AI. I'd put a couple of months' savings into a van and tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about Nadia's reaction to spending the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your wife say about the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask what happens if it fails. I'd say we keep two months back, and I keep the Keystone job until the firm pays a wage. She'd still give me a look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame for the cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. That's business. Companies cut costs, that's what they're for. The government should get out of the way of small firms, that's all I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. Then Keystone's not a career anymore, it's a stepping stone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: the office jobs are going, so get your hands on a trade. I'd tell younger lads at the mosque, don't do what I did, go and learn plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk is gone well before 2028 ends. But the repair firm has a few years after that, because robots for hands-on work come later. That's where I'd put everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full time with Yusuf within six months, learn plumbing properly through a fast course, and use AI to run the quotes and paperwork. I'd keep two months' savings as a floor and spend the rest on kit. Nadia's baking would carry the household while the firm got going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. But it's the kind of nervous where you get up early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says hands-on robots come about three years after AGI. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then that's three years to build something people trust. People still want a known face in their house, even if a robot could fix the boiler. I'd bet on being that face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your whole household riding on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the whole family. It'd be Nadia's baking and the firm, and both are run from our house. If those two go, that's when I'd worry properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before. Five years is enough to learn a trade, start something and do it right, without waiting for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at Keystone a bit longer, learn everything about how insurers will run claims with AI, then leave with that knowledge for the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Keystone two years, join the test team, and build the firm with Yusuf on weekends. In year three I'd go full time with a van, a plumbing qualification and a list of landlords from my Keystone days. We'd maybe buy a small house with a garage for the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Busy. Like the future's something I can shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about plans at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia wants children, and so do I. Five years means we could start a family once the firm pays a wage, maybe year three or four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be tempted to stay at Keystone if the new system made you valuable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'd know it doesn't last. That's what the five years tells you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, but calmer: build something, ten years is plenty if you start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do very well out of this one. I'd have the firm running long before AGI, with a name in town, and I'd be using AI for the office side the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Keystone three or four years and go for a senior handler role, then go full time with Yusuf. I'd take on an apprentice by year six. We'd have kids, buy a house, and maybe a second van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in that decade, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming for repair work, around 2039. But that's thirteen years away, and by then I'd want the firm to be managing jobs, not just doing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting too comfortable at Keystone. A good salary makes you lazy about a plan, so I'd keep the Saturday repair work going no matter what.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have a plan, but two years to build a trade from scratch is tight, and if it went wrong our savings are gone. What would help is fast, cheap trade courses and less red tape for starting a small firm, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll fix things when it all goes digital. Everyone talks about AI in offices. The pipes still burst.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI in offices. The pipes still burst.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** junior claims handler at Keystone, a landlord-only insurer.
He's married; his wife runs a **home baking business**, and they have about four months saved.
He uses **AI daily** and is first to try new systems, but still makes costly mistakes.
His **traditional, pro-enterprise** outlook leads him to a repair firm with his cousin rather than help.
As timelines shorten, he moves earlier into **hands-on work**, betting on trust.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is tight to build a trade from scratch.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, cheap **trade courses** and less red tape for **small firms**.
